chunks: With this chain, from 'Ammar ibn Musa, from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him)
Regarding the vessel from which nabid (fermented drink) is drunk, he said: 'Wash it seven times, and so is the dog.'
And regarding the man who was struck by thirst to the point of fearing for his life, and he consumed khamr (wine), he said: 'He drinks from it his sustenance (enough to survive).'
And he was asked about the table (m'aida) when the intoxicating wine was drunk upon it, he said: 'The table becomes prohibited (haram).'

And he was asked: If a man stands on a set table, eating from what is on it, and with the man is intoxicant but he has not yet poured it for anyone on it, he said: 'It does not become prohibited until it is drunk upon it.'
And if it is returned after it is drunk upon, then the faludhaj (a type of bread/dough), eat it, for it is another table.' He means: eat the faludhaj.
'And do not pray in a house that has khamr or intoxicant in it, because the angels do not enter it. And do not pray in a garment that has been touched by khamr or intoxicant until it is washed.'

He was asked about the nasuh (sprinkling water) that needs to be purified, how it is made so that it becomes permissible, he said: 'Take the water of the dates and boil it until two-thirds of the water of the dates disappears.'

And regarding two Christian men, one of them sold khamr or pigs to his companion, then they both embraced Islam before the dirhams were received, is the dirhams permissible for him? He said: 'There is no harm.'
And regarding the man who brings the drink and says: 'This is cooked (boiled) by one-third,' he said: 'If he is a pious and trustworthy Muslim, there is no harm in it being drunk.'

'Ammar said: I asked Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the man who is a Muslim and well-known, except that he drinks this nabid (intoxicant), he said: 'O 'Ammar, if he dies, do not pray over him (funeral prayer).'

key_terms.النَّبِيذُ: Nabid (fermented drink, often from dates or raisins)
key_terms.اَلْفَالُوذَجُ: Al-faludhaj (a type of bread or dough)

ai.seo_question: What are the Shia juristic rulings on washing vessels used for nabid and the permissibility of praying in rooms containing wine?
ai.summary: Compiled by Shaykh al-Tusi in *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, this hadith provides a comprehensive legal framework for handling intoxicants, emphasizing the distinction between *khamr* (wine) and *nabid* (fermented drink) through detailed purification rituals and ritual purity rules. It highlights the practical implications for daily worship, such as the validity of prayer in spaces or garments contaminated by intoxicants, and extends to social and economic aspects like the validity of trade before payment and the funeral prayer for habitual drinkers. The text underscores the Shia scholarly focus on both physical cleanliness and spiritual status, linking ritual purity to the presence of angels and the final judgment of the individual.
